title: Dental conditions, procedures and diagnostic terms in practice
objective: Distinguish common oral diseases, match them to the correct treatment terms, and interpret occlusion and radiograph vocabulary in clinical scenarios.
body:
Advanced terminology questions describe a patient and ask you to choose the condition, the procedure or the image that fits. Success depends on knowing what each term includes and, just as important, what it excludes.

**Caries and the pulp.** **Dental caries** is tooth decay caused when bacteria in **plaque** ferment sugars into acids that demineralize enamel. An early **white spot lesion** can remineralize with fluoride; once a cavity forms, it needs a **restoration**, such as a **composite** (tooth-colored resin) or **amalgam** (a metal alloy). If decay reaches the pulp, **pulpitis** results. **Reversible pulpitis** causes brief pain that stops when the stimulus is removed; **irreversible pulpitis** causes lingering or spontaneous pain and usually requires **root canal therapy** (endodontic treatment) or extraction. A collection of pus at the root tip is a **periapical abscess**.

**Gum disease.** **Gingivitis** is inflammation of the gingiva, with redness, swelling and bleeding, and it is reversible with good plaque control. **Periodontitis** involves loss of attachment and alveolar bone, shown by deepened **periodontal pockets**. Hardened plaque is **calculus** (tartar), removed by **scaling**; smoothing root surfaces is **root planing**.

**Replacing and covering teeth.**
- **Crown**: a cap covering the entire visible tooth.
- **Fixed bridge**: a false tooth (**pontic**) attached to crowns on neighboring **abutment** teeth.
- **Implant**: a post placed in bone that supports a crown.
- **Denture**: a removable replacement, complete or partial.

**Occlusion.** **Occlusion** is how upper and lower teeth meet; **malocclusion** is a faulty bite. Angle's classification uses the first molars: **Class I** has a normal molar relationship (crowding may still exist), **Class II** has the lower molar positioned distally, often with a retruded chin, and **Class III** has the lower molar positioned mesially, often with a prominent chin (**prognathism**). Other bite terms include **overjet** (horizontal overlap), **overbite** (vertical overlap) and **crossbite**.

**Radiographs.** A **bitewing** shows the crowns of upper and lower posterior teeth together and is used to detect caries between teeth. A **periapical** image shows an entire tooth, including the root tip. A **panoramic** image shows both jaws, the sinuses and the temporomandibular joints on one film. On radiographs, dense structures such as enamel and metal appear **radiopaque** (light), while decay and soft tissue appear **radiolucent** (dark).

The most common mistake students make is treating gingivitis and periodontitis as the same disease. Bleeding alone points to gingivitis; bone loss and attachment loss are what make it periodontitis.
examples: A patient with bleeding gums but normal pocket depths and no bone loss on radiographs has gingivitis, not periodontitis.
A three-unit bridge replacing tooth 19 uses teeth 18 and 20 as abutments and a pontic in the 19 position.
An amalgam filling appears bright white (radiopaque) on a bitewing, while recurrent decay beneath it appears dark (radiolucent).

questions.stem: A patient reports a throbbing toothache that wakes him at night and lasts long after a hot drink. Which term best fits?
questions.explanation: Spontaneous, lingering pain points to irreversible pulpitis. Reversible pulpitis is the main distractor, but its pain is brief and stops when the stimulus is removed.

questions.stem: Which radiograph would a dentist choose to check for decay between the back teeth of both arches at once?
questions.explanation: Bitewings show upper and lower posterior crowns together and are the standard for interproximal caries. A panoramic image shows both jaws but with less detail for small proximal lesions.

questions.stem: A hygienist records 5 mm pockets and the radiograph shows horizontal bone loss. Which diagnosis term fits?
questions.explanation: Pocketing with bone loss means loss of attachment, which defines periodontitis. Gingivitis involves inflamed gums without bone or attachment loss.

questions.stem: In a three-unit fixed bridge, what is the artificial tooth that replaces the missing one?
questions.explanation: The pontic is the suspended replacement tooth. Abutments are the natural teeth or implants that support the bridge, the most common confusion.

questions.stem: An orthodontist notes the patient's lower first molars are positioned mesially relative to the upper first molars and the chin is prominent. Which classification is this?
questions.explanation: Class III means the mandibular molar is mesial, often with prognathism. Class II is the reverse, with the lower molar distal and the chin often retruded.

questions.stem: On a bitewing, a dark shadow appears under the edge of an existing metal filling. How is this area described?
questions.explanation: Decay is less dense, lets X-rays pass, and appears dark, or radiolucent. The metal filling itself is radiopaque, which is why that term is tempting but wrong for the shadow.

questions.stem: A child's front teeth stick out horizontally far beyond the lower incisors when biting. Which term describes this horizontal overlap?
questions.explanation: Overjet is horizontal projection of upper incisors beyond the lower ones. Overbite is vertical overlap, the closest distractor.

questions.stem: After scaling, a hygienist smooths the root surfaces below the gumline to help the tissue reattach. What is this procedure called?
questions.explanation: Root planing smooths cementum after calculus removal. An apicoectomy is surgical removal of the root tip, an unrelated endodontic surgery.

flashcards.definition: Pulp inflammation with lingering or spontaneous pain that will not heal on its own; usually treated with root canal therapy or extraction.
The artificial tooth in a fixed bridge that replaces a missing tooth.
Image showing upper and lower posterior crowns together, used to detect decay between teeth.
Appearing dark on a radiograph because X-rays pass through, as with decay or soft tissue.
Angle class in which the mandibular first molar is mesial to the maxillary first molar, often with a prominent chin.
